subject: Biotechnology
title: Microfluidics for Synbio
description: A short lesson to help you apply Microfluidics for Synbio.

hook.text: Shrink the lab to a chip — microfluidics handles nanoliter reactions, testing millions of designs on a thumbnail.

buildup.text: Droplet microfluidics encapsulates single cells in tiny water-in-oil droplets — each is a separate experiment.

discovery.text: Millions of enzyme variants are screened per hour — directed evolution in droplets is a thousand times faster.

twist.text: Cross-contamination between droplets is nearly zero — each picoreactor is chemically isolated from its neighbors.

climax.text: Organ-on-a-chip combines microfluidics with living cells — testing drugs on miniature human tissues before clinical trials.

punchline.text: Tiny channels, massive throughput — microfluidics is synbio's accelerator.

quiz.question: How does droplet microfluidics enable high-throughput screening?
options: It uses large bioreactors divided into sections
Single cells are encapsulated in isolated nanoliter droplets, each acting as a separate experiment
It mixes all variants together and tests them simultaneously

details.summary: Microfluidics manipulates tiny fluid volumes in channels thinner than a human hair, enabling high-throughput screening of millions of synthetic biology constructs. Droplet-based systems encapsulate individual cells in picoliter droplets for rapid testing of genetic variants.
details.whyItMatters: Synthetic biology generates enormous libraries of genetic variants that must be screened for desired function. Microfluidics tests millions of variants per day using minimal reagents, dramatically accelerating the design-build-test-learn cycle.
takeaways: Microfluidic chips process thousands of reactions per second in tiny channels
Droplet systems encapsulate single cells for high-throughput screening
Miniaturization reduces reagent costs by a thousand-fold or more

faq.question: How does droplet-based microfluidics work for screening?
faq.answer: Individual cells are encapsulated in water-in-oil droplets at rates of thousands per second. Each droplet acts as a tiny independent reactor where the cell grows and produces products. Droplets are sorted by fluorescence or other signals to isolate high-performing variants.

faq.question: What advantages does microfluidics offer over traditional screening?
faq.answer: Microfluidics screens millions of variants per day versus thousands with robotics. It uses nanoliter volumes, reducing reagent costs by orders of magnitude. Precise environmental control enables experiments impossible at macro scale. Single-cell resolution eliminates population averaging.
